questions.questionText: When does a Java Stream pipeline actually process its elements?
questions.explanation: Stream operations like filter() and map() are lazy — they just describe a pipeline. Nothing runs until a terminal operation (collect(), forEach(), count(), etc.) is invoked.

answers.answerText: Only when a terminal operation like collect() or forEach() is called
Immediately when filter() or map() is called
As soon as the stream is created from a collection
Only when the JVM garbage collector runs

questions.explanation: groupingBy(classifier) partitions a stream into a Map<K, List<T>> keyed by the classifier function — the functional equivalent of SQL's GROUP BY, optionally paired with a downstream collector to aggregate each group.

answers.answerText: Groups stream elements into a Map keyed by a classifier function
Sorts a stream's elements into ascending order
Removes duplicate elements from a stream
Splits a stream into parallel and sequential halves

entries.topicDescription: Choosing the right List, Set, and Map implementation and using them correctly.

questions.questionText: Why does ArrayList usually outperform LinkedList in practice, even for insertions?
questions.explanation: ArrayList's contiguous array layout is far more cache-friendly than LinkedList's scattered nodes, which usually outweighs LinkedList's theoretical O(1) mid-list insertion advantage in real-world benchmarks.

answers.answerText: Its contiguous memory layout is much more cache-friendly
ArrayList never needs to resize its backing array
LinkedList cannot store more than 1000 elements
ArrayList insertions are O(1) in the middle of the list

questions.questionText: What happens if a class overrides equals() but not hashCode()?
questions.explanation: HashMap uses hashCode() to find a key's bucket and equals() to confirm the match within it. Without a consistent hashCode(), two equals()-equal keys can land in different buckets, so put()/get() silently fail to find each other.

answers.answerText: HashMap lookups can silently fail even for equals()-equal keys
The code fails to compile
equals() automatically generates a matching hashCode()
Nothing — hashCode() is never used by collections

entries.topicDescription: Checked vs unchecked exceptions, try-with-resources, and designing exception hierarchies.

questions.questionText: What's the key difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions (extending Exception, not RuntimeException) must be caught or declared with 'throws' — the compiler enforces it. Unchecked exceptions (extending RuntimeException) require no such declaration.

answers.answerText: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked ones don't
Unchecked exceptions can only be thrown from static methods
Checked exceptions are always fatal to the JVM
There is no real difference in modern Java

questions.questionText: In what order are multiple resources closed in a try-with-resources block?
questions.explanation: Resources are closed in the reverse of their declaration order — mirroring how nested finally blocks would unwind by hand.

answers.answerText: In reverse of their declaration order
In the same order they were declared
In an unspecified, JVM-dependent order
All at once, in parallel

entries.topicDescription: Threads, the executor framework, and the memory-visibility rules that make concurrent code correct.

questions.questionText: Why prefer an ExecutorService over creating raw Threads directly?
questions.explanation: A raw Thread per task is expensive and uncapped — nothing stops a burst of work from creating thousands of OS threads. An ExecutorService reuses a bounded pool of worker threads instead.

answers.answerText: It reuses a bounded pool instead of creating unlimited OS threads
Raw Threads cannot run more than once
ExecutorService is required for any I/O operation
Threads created directly cannot be interrupted

questions.questionText: Besides mutual exclusion, what else does a 'synchronized' block guarantee?
questions.explanation: synchronized establishes a happens-before relationship: writes made before releasing a lock are guaranteed visible to any thread that later acquires the same lock — solving the memory-visibility problem, not just preventing concurrent execution.

answers.answerText: Memory visibility of writes made before the lock was released
That the JVM will never garbage-collect the locked object
That the block will run on the main thread
That exceptions inside it are automatically retried

entries.topicDescription: Type parameters, wildcards, and why generics are erased at runtime.

questions.questionText: What is type erasure in Java generics?
questions.explanation: Generic type parameters exist only at compile time for type checking; the compiler erases them afterward, so List<String> and List<Integer> compile to the identical bytecode at runtime.

answers.answerText: Generic type information is removed by the compiler after type-checking
Generics are converted into reflection calls at runtime
Unused generic classes are deleted from the compiled jar
Type parameters are replaced with random unique class names

questions.questionText: Under the PECS mnemonic, when should you use a '? extends T' wildcard?
questions.explanation: 'Producer Extends' — use '? extends T' when the collection only ever produces values you read, since the compiler can't safely allow adding to it without knowing the exact runtime subtype.

answers.answerText: When the parameter only produces values you read from it
When the parameter only consumes values you write into it
When T must be a primitive type
When the collection must be thread-safe
